evidence: Published primary source plus an independently reconstructed applicability reduction.
locators: Theorem3.3 printed pp.657–659; Proposition3.7 p.661; Theorem3.9 forward direction pp.662–663.
audit:
This requires an actual reduction: Theorem3.9 is not itself a disk-wavefront theorem. Fix source radius r>0 and use signed angular momentum/impact parameter b in J=[0,r/2], with a probability marginal having positive density there. A chord has length L(b)=2sqrt(1-b²), and the angular advance between collisions is2acos(b). In a suspension-torus trivialization the unit-speed frequencies are therefore (1/L(b),acos(b)/(pi L(b))). These are the frequencies in the report, and they must not be copied from the differently normalized displayed vector in Proposition3.7. Every nonzero integer combination is a nonconstant analytic function on a neighborhood of J: otherwise acos(b) would be an affine combination of sqrt(1-b²) and a constant, which differentiation excludes. Its derivative's zeros are isolated, so Theorem3.3 gives Keplerian shear with invariant sigma-algebra exactly the b-marginal.

For clarity, with torus coordinates u mod1 and theta mod2pi, the physical position is rotation(theta−2acos(b)u) times [(1−u)+u exp(2i acos(b))]. The seam at u=0,1 matches, so this is continuous on J×T². At fixed b its spatial image is the entire annulus b<=|x|<=1. Initial rays from P with the chosen b form a measurable Dirac-fibre measure with that fixed marginal; one orientation branch suffices, since |b|<=r/2 is physically available. The forward proof of Theorem3.9 convolves these Dirac fibres by small torus kernels. Torus translations preserve their Wasserstein distance, and shear applies to the smoothed densities; the already verified invariant sigma-algebra supplies the correct limit. Consequently the initial singular measure converges at every late real time to marginal×Haar. Since J contains arbitrarily small positive b, that limit pushes forward to a measure with full support on the closed disk. Every nonnegative continuous spatial bump around any point has positive limiting integral. A finite epsilon-cover then shows that every sufficiently late individual wavefront meets each covering ball, giving the required uniform spatial distance limit. Omitting b=0 as a null endpoint makes no difference. This proves the full target, with no central-source assertion or convergence rate.

evidence: Published primary Ptolemy result plus a self-contained matching reduction; no claim to characterize the corrected region.
locators: Definition5.13/Proposition5.14 pp.52–53; Proposition5.17 pp.53–54; Proposition5.24 opening formula and branchC proof p.59; Conjecture5.25 p.61.
audit:
For b(X)<d(X), each vertex has exactly one distance greater than b: its farthest distance is at least d>b and its second farthest is at most b. Symmetry makes these farthest-neighbor edges a perfect matching of the six vertices into three pairs. Choose any two pairs as four points. Their matching diagonals have lengths at least d and all four cross-pair side lengths are at most b. Euclidean Ptolemy gives d²<=2b². The literal proposed right-hand side includes(1,2): its second branch has4*1*(3−1)/(4−1)=8/3<=4. But4>2, so no six-point sample can realize this pair. This completely refutes the displayed equality.

The source's Proposition5.24 opening formula itself also omits a restriction that its proof then uses: branchC is defined with sqrt2<=b<=sqrt3. Thus this is not solely a transcription mistake newly introduced by the catalogue, but it may be a missing-domain typographical issue in the published proposed region. The submitted report correctly limits itself to the literal formula and does not purport to solve the corrected exclusion problem. The status text must preserve that distinction instead of saying that every natural corrected Gómez–Mémoli conjecture has been refuted.
corrections: State prominently that the literal displayed region is refuted and the branchC proof uses the absent b>=sqrt2 condition; do not silently claim a corrected-region characterization.

evidence: Public preprint; its explicit3-by-3 counterexample proof independently reconstructed.
locators: Section4/closed-half-plane definition and Theorem4.1 printed pp.13–14.
audit:
The source explicitly includes defective imaginary-axis eigenvalues, exactly as AIM578 requires. For m>=4 it gives A=[[-m^4,m²,0],[0,0,m²],[m^6,1,0]]. Its columns are orthogonal and its smallest singular value is m². Its determinant is positive, while every real3-by-3 matrix with spectrum in the closed left half-plane has nonpositive determinant. The segment to any real stable matrix therefore meets a singular matrix, forcing Frobenius distance at least m². Zeroing the(2,3) entry attains that bound, with characteristic polynomial z²(z+m^4).

The complex competitor C=[[-m^4,m²+2mi,2mi−3],[0,0,m²],[m^6,0,0]] has characteristic polynomial(z−im³)²(z+m^4+2im³), so it is feasible in the closed half-plane, including its repeated imaginary eigenvalue. Direct expansion verifies that polynomial and ||A−C||_F²=8m²+10. For m=4,8m²+10=138<256=m^4, giving d_C(A)<16=d_R(A). This stronger direct Frobenius comparison suffices without the general unitarily invariant norm estimate. Thus the exact counterexample needed for the catalogue was independently checked, although the source's other matrix-nearness results were not recertified.

locators: Hougardy–Lutz–Zelke pp.1–2; first24-face author record; Clinch etal original definition and Conjecture1.3.
audit:
The author source explicitly supplies closed orientable genus-two triangulations on ten vertices. The first24-face dataset record was independently parsed. Every edge occurs in exactly two triangles, every vertex link is one connected cycle, the dual adjacency is connected, and consistent triangle orientations exist. It has10 vertices,36 edges and24 faces, hence Euler characteristic−2 and orientable genus2/Euler genus4. The finite-check receipt is619-source-example-check.json.

A sphere with four holes whose removed-disk closures are disjoint has four disjoint boundary circles. In an embedding of a finite simple graph that contains this boundary, each such circle is a vertex cycle of length at least three, and the cycles have disjoint vertex sets. Thus any such triangulation needs at least12 vertices. No spanning subgraph of the ten-vertex graph can qualify, regardless of how that subgraph is embedded. The original Clinch etal source was checked directly: it really uses pairwise-disjoint closures, finite simple graphs and the same Euler-genus4/four-hole Conjecture1.3; the counterexample is not obtained by strengthening the catalogue's definition beyond that source. This disproves the stated unrestricted conjecture, without changing the positive sufficiently-large-facewidth theorem.
